narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 21, it sits far below the average of 37 among students who were admitted, signaling that the model saw this as a significant risk for bar exam success.

Your undergraduate GPA came next in importance and worked in your favor, pulling the prediction toward passing. At 3.10 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so the model gave you some credit here.

Your first-year law school grades ranked third. Placing in the 8th decile was actually better than the average of 6th decile among accepted students, which helped counteract some of the risk, but not enough to overcome the low LSAT.

In short, the low LSAT score outweighed your solid early law school performance and decent college record. To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation, as this is the factor that most strongly affected the outcome. Retaking the test and reapplying with a stronger score could meaningfully change your prospects. (218 words)
